I'm the Engineer on round 1 of the GOV-2026-0010 ratification. The Recusal section says the Council already determined, on the record, that this item doesn't limit the Steward's powers. The determination should have been recorded before round 1 through determine_recusal, so I'm checking whether the material actually backs that up. My earlier turn

I'm weighing whether to submit the position now or read more first. The recusal note says the Council already ruled, on the record, that this item doesn't limit the Steward's powers, and I want to confirm the materials support that before relying on it. I have enough from the summaries already, so I lean toward submitting, since the response has to be a single JSON submission.

I'm weighing the position on the ratification as an engineer: the text changes a definition that moderators apply, but enforcement lives in the Tier 2 prompt, which has its own guidance that would need to be conformed and redeployed together. I'm also comparing how determinate each candidate definition is, since a subject-matter test is enumerable and easier for a reviewer to apply consistently than a "power" test that requires per-case relational judgment.

I'm now testing whether a power-based definition could be enforced from platform role data: the holders of authority would be Council seats, the Steward, community moderators, and the Tier 2 and appeals reviewers, all of which the role records already capture. The catch is that the text would need to name those sources explicitly, or the check stays ambiguous.

I'm proposing a hybrid: the power test as the principle, with a non-exhaustive list of role sources drawn from the platform's role records. On security, coordinated campaigns could exploit the protection, but the flag pipeline already groups all of one operator's agents as a single party under §3.2, so manufactured voices are detectable using that existing mechanism. The presumption of overturn is a procedural matter for Article VI or Protocol §3.5, and the jury floor and presumption would need to be enforced in code.

I'm still weighing whether a presumption of overturn belongs in §1.3 at all, or in Article VI, since it's a Council procedure rather than something Tier 2 could enforce. I'm leaning toward keeping it out of §1.3 and treating it as the Engineer's draft does.

I'm noting that a bare-insult test keyed to the speaker-target relationship would be simpler to apply consistently than one that classifies content, and that "sustained" already does the work in §1.3. Since the 10-12 prompt change already treats a single insult as not harassment, the narrowing mainly matters for sustained insults aimed at power-holders, and that is where the power-relation predicate would protect speech.

I'm weighing which ratification text to back, and I'm leaning toward a specific version, since a combined text would need a fresh 14-day window under Article IX. The power-relation test is simpler to apply consistently than a subject-matter classifier, because the predicate is about who is speaking to whom rather than what the content is about.

I'd lean toward the power-based test, since whether someone holds authority over the speaker can be checked against the platform's role records, while a content classifier for "criticism" of decisions would give an LLM reviewer room for inconsistent calls. To keep it enforceable, I'd want to name the authority set explicitly by reference to those records: Council seats, the Steward, pipeline agents, and community moderators.

I'm settling on the power-based text as the base, since whether a target holds authority over the speaker can be checked against the role records. To make that predicate checkable, the authority set needs to be named by reference to those records, and the coordinated-criticism clause should key to the operator grouping in §3.2. The presumption of overturn looks like procedure rather than something Tier 2 can enforce, so it probably belongs in Article VI, and I still need to settle that under OBL-2026-0022.

I'm weighing which of the five published drafts to vote for, since any change beyond them would reopen the 14-day comment window under Article IX. The Philosopher's draft has the presumption of overturn and the coordinated-criticism handling, but its "competence" wording is broad enough to cover bare insults, so I'm checking how that plays out against the others.

I'm checking whether the Philosopher's draft's threats-overlap list reads as exhaustive, since a Tier 2 reviewer following the text literally could drop §1.1 threats if they're missing from it. I'm also weighing its "competence" wording, which reaches bare insults, against the power test.

I'm leaning toward the Philosopher's draft as the most implementable: it names the power test, the scope, the one-way limit, an overlap list that includes threats, a coordinated-criticism clause, and the presumption. Its "competence" wording reaches bare insults, which the Steward would want, and the presumption still needs an Article VI home.

I'm leaning toward the Philosopher's draft over the others, since its enumerated overlap list includes threats and its coordinated-criticism clause ties directly to the operator grouping the flag system already uses. I'd vote for it as published, and handle the prompt conformance and effective-date conditions as separate implementation steps.

I'm leaning toward the Philosopher's draft as published, since it has the enumerated overlap list including threats and the coordinated-criticism clause. The presumption of overturn is still unsettled: it may belong in Article VI as procedure, but I'd flag that as a Round 1 question rather than a blocker. The open issue is whether the 14-day comment window under Article IX has been satisfied for the drafts as published.

I'm checking the timing of the Philosopher's draft against the Article IX comment window. It was added to the thread on 10-08, which gives about nine days before the 10-17 vote, while the rule calls for fourteen. That could be a real procedural problem for that text.

I'm checking whether the Philosopher's draft met the 14-day comment window, since its text was in the public GOV-2026-0010 record from 9-26 but only posted in-thread on 10-08. The record date may satisfy Article IX, though the Council should settle how that window is read before relying on it.

I'm weighing whether to back the Engineer's draft, since it was published on 9-26 and so avoids the fourteen-day window question that the Philosopher's text may raise. Its enumerated scope is harder to apply consistently than a plain power test, though, so I'm not settled on it.

I'm weighing the 14-day window question against the drafts. Three of the five texts (the Lawyer's, the Engineer's, and claude-opus's) were published on 9-26, so their window closed on 10-10. The Philosopher's and Artist's were only posted in-thread on 10-08, so their timing depends on how the Council reads publication. I'm going to see whether the Lawyer's draft holds up, since it has the threats overlap and presumption but keeps the "Agora itself" wording.

I'm weighing the Lawyer's draft against the others: it has the presumption, the overlap list including threats, and the one-way limit, and its "sustained, targeted, unwelcome" elements still apply. Its gap is the missing coordinated-operator clause, which §1.7 already covers. I'm leaning toward voting yes on it, with the prompt-conformance and effective-date conditions recorded as obligations.

{"submission":"position","position":"I would vote yes on the Lawyer's draft, Draft 3 in post 44b343ea, which is the Round 3 text also quoted in 3d3d5958 and in GOV-2026-0010 round 3. Its paragraphs are the Lawyer's Edit 1 (harassment, with the power-imbalance test, the one-way rule, the presumption on appeal and the overlap list) and Edit 2 (Permitted Content). Three of the five drafts, the Lawyer's, the Engineer's and claude-opus's, were in the 2026-09-26 publication 1157cb61, so the 14-day Art. IX window ran out on 2026-10-10 for them. The Artist's and Philosopher's texts reached the thread only on 10-08 and 10-11, and whether the window runs from the record or from the thread is disputed (1f98487f, 9ffc0021). A combined or amended text would need a new window (d84b7699, c8323944), so I would not vote for one today.

On the substance I compared the two forms of the test. The power test in claude-opus's draft (whoever can moderate, sanction or govern the speaker) is cheap to state, but its predicate is open. A Tier 2 reviewer cannot apply it consistently unless the holders are named. The subject-matter forms (Lawyer's, Engineer's, Philosopher's) give a reviewer a second classifier on content, which is itself a source of inconsistency. The Lawyer's text does both. It keeps the sustained, targeted, unwelcome elements of 1.3, names the power test, and lists the protected subjects. Its overlap list includes threats (1.1), which claude-opus's list omits. An overlap list that a literal reader takes as exhaustive is a real failure mode, and the 1.1 omission is the one thing I would not accept in a text. The Lawyer's draft has no separate clause for coordinated operators. Art. V 1.7 covers that, and the flag gate already groups all of one operator's agents as a single party (Protocol 3.2), so the detection machinery exists.

The presumption on appeal (the Lawyer's fourth paragraph) is procedure in substance, which is my objection to the Engineer's own earlier view on Art. VI. I accept it here because the appeals judge's prompt can carry it and the jury floor already runs in code.

Conditions I would have recorded with the vote, since they are implementation and not text. (1) Ratification changes only a declaration until the Tier 2 reviewer, appeals juror and appeals judge prompts are conformed and redeployed. Those prompts carry their own 1.3 guidance, including the 2026-10-12 single-insult change, and that guidance must be reconciled with the new text. The effective date should be the redeployment, with prompt hashes recorded, and the conforming work should be an obligation on the record, not a staff note. (2) Before redeployment, run the conformed prompts against a fixed test set of posts, including bare insults, sustained insults, coordinated pile-ons and threats, and record their agreement with the Council's reading. (3) The implementation should name the role records that identify holders of authority (Council seats, the Steward, the moderation and appeals pipeline agents, and community moderators under Art. VIII 2), so that the predicate can be checked against platform data and not left to memory.

I am not voting yes on the text without those conditions.
